A.Berger |synonyms_ref = }} '''''Graptopetalum paraguayense''''' is a species of [[succulent plant]] in the [[jade plant]] family, [[Crassulaceae]], that is native to [[Tamaulipas]], [[Mexico]]."Botanica. The Illustrated AZ of over 10000 garden plants and how to cultivate them", pp. 410-411. Könemann, 2004. {{ISBN|3-8331-1253-0}} Common names include '''mother-of-pearl-plant''' and '''ghost plant'''. This is not to be confused with ''[[Monotropa uniflora]]'' which is also referred to as the “Ghost plant”. ''G. paraguayense'' has white flowers which have a form of a star. The Graptopetalum paraguayense is called the ghost plant because of the residue on the leaves making it look like a ghost. ==Description== The plant has a spreading and creeping habit that reaches 20 cm high by 60 cm wide. Its appearance may vary depending on the soil and the exposure. The hanging rod can reach up to 2 m in length and a thickness of 2 cm. Green to light grey leaves can be up to 7 cm long and 3 cm wide. Thick and fleshy, they are arranged in a spiral around the stem and are very easily detached from the [[Rosette (botany)|rosette]], that is why this plant has been nicknamed "porcelain [[succulent]]". Its flowers appearing in spring have five white [[petal]]s spotted with red. ==Cultivation and uses== This hardy plant stands temperatures down to −10 °C. If it is sheltered from rain and too much humidity, it is easy to grow in [[temperate climate]]s. It is readily propagated by [[cuttings (plant)|cutting]] leaves or stems. It supports both full sun and partial shade. Watering should be avoided in the event of excessive heat. It is often used as an [[ornamental plant]] in gardens. Plants of this species are a functional food, being used as edible vegetables.{{cite journal | last1=Jaiswal | first1=Varun | last2=Lee | first2=Hae-Jeung | title=A Comprehensive Review on Graptopetalum paraguayense's Phytochemical Profiles, Pharmacological Activities, and Development as a Functional Food | journal=Plants | date=2025 | volume=14 | issue=3 | page=349 | doi=10.3390/plants14030349 | doi-access=free | pmid=39942910 | pmc=11820263 | bibcode=2025Plnts..14..349J }} This species is also valued for its antihypertensive and hepatoprotective activities in traditional Taiwanese and Chinese medicine. ==Gallery== File:Suculenta1.jpg|Potted plants File:(MHNT) Graptopetalum paraguayense Flower.jpg|Flowers File:Graptopetalum paraguayense 20151011-2.JPG|In a clump File:Graptopetalum paraguayense - Serres d'Auteuil.JPG|Rosette File:Graptopetalum paraguayense - Buffalo Botanical Gardens.jpg|[[Buffalo and Erie County Botanical Gardens]] File:Graptopetalum paraguayense 3.jpg|Graptosedum Ghosty, often confused with its parent Graptopetalum Paraguayense.{{cite web | url=https://www.crassulaceae.ch/de/artikel?akID=60&aaID=2&aiID=G&aID=1281 | title=Ghosty '고스티' }} File:Graptopetalum paraguayense at Hotel Nikko breakfast buffet Kaohsiung May 2026.jpg|Edible succulent leaves in a salad bar in Taiwan ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Wikispecies-inline|Graptopetalum paraguayense|''Graptopetalum paraguayense''}} {{Commons category|Graptopetalum paraguayense|position=left}} {{Taxonbar|from=Q3574180}} [[Category:Graptopetalum|paraguayense]] [[Category:Endemic flora of Mexico]] [[Category:Flora of Tamaulipas]] [[Category:Plants described in 1938]] [[Category:Garden plants of North America]] [[Category:Drought-tolerant plants]] [[Category:Taxa named by N.
